blocks.text: Predicate logic is an extension of propositional logic. It lets us express more detailed statements about objects and their properties, and talk about individuals, groups and the relationships between them (Fig 2.7).

blocks.title: Predicate
blocks.text: A predicate is a statement that can be true or false depending on the values of its variables; it describes a property of an object or a relationship between objects.

For example, 'x is greater than 5' is a predicate because its truth depends on x. Predicate logic can express statements such as 'All students are hardworking' or 'Some books are interesting', so it is used to represent knowledge formally.

blocks.caption: Propositional logic and predicate logic
rows: Whole statements that are true or false
Objects, their properties and relationships, using predicates and variables
A = 'Ali is tall' (cannot see inside A)
Tall(Ali): the subject Ali and the property Tall
More expressive and flexible; covers many objects and conditions

blocks.text: Predicates describe properties or relationships of objects; for example isEven(x) is true if x is an even number, and Helps(x, y) can mean 'x helps y'. Variables represent objects or values from the domain of discourse. With variables we can write general statements such as 'for all x, x > 0'. Together, predicates and variables form predicate-logic expressions that state complex ideas clearly and formally.

blocks.alt: Left panel: a box Helps(x, y) labelled predicate: x helps y, with lines down to two circles x and y, each labelled variable; note: Helps(Ali, Sara) is true or false once x and y are given values. Right panel: propositional, A = 'Ali is tall', one letter that cannot see inside, limited; predicate, Tall(Ali), subject Ali plus property Tall, and Tall(Sara) or Tall(x) use the same predicate, much more expressive.
blocks.caption: The structure of a predicate, and propositional versus predicate form (original diagram after Fig 2.7).
blocks.long_description: A predicate is like a sentence with blanks; filling the blanks with objects turns it into a proposition that is true or false.
